readingInstruction: Read Revelation 16:1-21. The seven bowls of God’s wrath are poured out in a rapid series, resembling the plagues of Egypt. Notice the repeated refusal to repent, the declaration that God’s judgments are just, and the final cry, “It is done!”
settingTheScene: The bowls are the last of the series of seven (seals, trumpets, bowls). They are described as final, bringing the wrath of God to completion. Unlike the trumpets, which affected a third of the earth, the bowls are total. Interpreters differ on whether the three series are sequential, parallel, or progressively intensifying cycles that cover the same period from different angles. In any reading, the point is the same: God’s judgment on the beast’s kingdom is just and certain, and he will bring evil to account.
observation: “Go and pour out on the earth the seven bowls of the wrath of God” (v. 1).
“Harmful and painful sores came upon the people who bore the mark of the beast” (v. 2).
“Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!” (v. 7).
“They did not repent and give him glory” (v. 9).
“Its water was dried up, to prepare the way for the kings from the east” (v. 12).
“Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake” (v. 15).
“And they assembled them at the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon” (v. 16).
interpretation:
A loud voice from the temple commands the seven angels to pour out the bowls. The first brings sores on those with the mark of the beast, like the boils of Egypt. The second turns the sea to blood, killing every living thing in it. The third turns the rivers and springs to blood, and the angel of the waters declares: “Just are you, O Holy One, who is and who was, for you brought these judgments. For they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. It is what they deserve!” A voice from the altar adds, “Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!” This is the answer to the martyrs’ cry in 6:10: God’s judgments are retributive, matched to the sin. The fourth bowl scorches people with fire from the sun, “and they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. They did not repent and give him glory.” This is the tragic refrain: even under judgment, hearts remain hard. The fifth falls on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom is plunged into darkness; people gnaw their tongues in anguish and curse God, but do not repent of their deeds.

The sixth bowl dries up the great river Euphrates “to prepare the way for the kings from the east.” Three unclean spirits like frogs come from the mouths of the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet, performing signs and going out to assemble the kings of the whole world “for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.” Then the voice interrupts: “Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed!” This is a call to watchfulness in the midst of the vision. “And they assembled them at the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon.” The name probably means “Mount of Megiddo,” a site of famous battles in Israel’s history (Judges 5; 2 Kings 23:29), though Megiddo is a plain, not a mountain, so it is a symbolic name for the place where the final battle is gathered. Interpreters differ on whether this is a literal military conflict at the end of history or a symbol of the final spiritual confrontation between the forces of evil and God. Notice that in the account no battle is described here; it is deferred to 19:19-21, where the beast and the kings gather against the rider on the white horse, and the battle is won by his word.

The seventh bowl is poured into the air, and a loud voice from the throne says, “It is done!” Flashes of lightning, rumblings, thunder, and a great earthquake, such as there has never been, split the great city into three parts, and the cities of the nations fall. “God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath.” Every island flees, mountains vanish, and great hailstones, about a hundred pounds each, fall from heaven on people, and they curse God. The chapter ends as it began, with human hearts unrepentant.

This chapter is hard to read. We should neither dwell on it with relish nor skip over it. It tells us that God takes evil seriously. The same Lord who offers mercy will not let evil go unanswered. It also tells us something about the human heart: apart from grace, even the experience of God’s judgment does not produce repentance. We need new hearts, and Christ gives them.
connection: Exodus 7-10 recounts the plagues of Egypt. Psalm 79:1-3 and Isaiah 49:26 relate to those who shed blood. Genesis 9:6 and Luke 11:49-51 speak of the blood of the prophets. Isaiah 11:15-16 and Jeremiah 50:38 describe drying up the Euphrates. Judges 5:19 and 2 Kings 23:29-30 mention Megiddo. Ezekiel 38-39 describes a final assault against God’s people. Matthew 24:43-44 and 1 Thessalonians 5:2-4 describe the coming as a thief. Revelation 19:11-21 shows the final battle. John 19:30, “It is finished.” Romans 2:4-5 speaks of an unrepentant heart.
application:
Stay awake: think of one habit that helps you stay alert and watchful in your faith, and strengthen it this week.

Pray for someone with a hard heart, that God would grant repentance.

When you are struck by the justice of God’s judgments, thank Christ for taking the wrath for those who trust in him.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that his judgments are true and just.
Ask him to give you a tender heart that repents.
Thank him that he hears the blood of his saints.
